title: If You Are Looking for a Husband, Try the Midwest
gist: Using the IFS Marriage Map, Danielle Franz argues that the Midwest holds the largest geographic concentration of eligible (single, full-time-employed) men, that having employed single men around predicts women's marriage rates better than sheer numbers of single men, and that local culture—not just dating-market math—drives where marriage flourishes.

insights.claim: Filtering the IFS Marriage Map for men ages 22-39 with full-time employment shows the Midwest as the largest geographic concentration of eligible men, though pockets of high density exist across the country.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Geographic clustering of marriage-market fundamentals maps onto regional household-formation and housing-demand differences worth tracking.
insights.quote: the Midwest represented the largest geographic concentration of eligible men by the standards I selected
insights.locator: The map lit up with varying shades

insights.claim: For Americans ages 22-29, many of the highest marriage-rate regions are in the interior, while eight of the 10 lowest-rate regions are in the New York and Los Angeles metropolitan areas.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Coastal metros lag interior regions in young-adult marriage, a demographic split with downstream consequences for regional consumer and housing markets.
insights.quote: eight of the 10 lowest-rate regions are in the New York and Los Angeles metropolitan areas

insights.claim: Coastal metros that rank lowest for marriage among twenty-somethings rise to the top among thirty-somethings, indicating the coastal gap is partly a matter of delayed timing rather than absence of marriage.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: The age at which coastal versus interior marriage occurs shifts the timing of family-linked spending, not just its incidence.
insights.quote: Among thirty-somethings, those same coastal metros make their way to the top.

insights.claim: For women ages 22-39, having many single full-time-employed men nearby is more predictive of marriage rates than simply having many single men around.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Male labor-force attachment, not raw sex ratios, is the operative marriage-market variable—linking male employment trends to family formation.
insights.quote: simply having lots of single men around isn't as predictive of marriage rates as having lots of single, full-time-employed men around
insights.locator: Of course, I had smuggled one rather important qualification

insights.claim: Living somewhere with more single men earning at least $60,000 is strongly associated with marriage rates among women in their thirties, but that relationship essentially vanishes for women in their twenties.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Earnings thresholds matter more for later marriages, suggesting women marrying younger bet on future rather than realized male earning potential.
insights.quote: living somewhere with more single men earning at least $60,000 is strongly associated with marriage rates among women in their thirties

insights.claim: Even within the Midwest, some markets underperform: filtering for single men in their twenties employed full time turns much of Illinois red on the map.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Marriage-market strength varies within regions, cautioning against treating whole regions as uniform demographic blocks.
insights.quote: Illinois, for example. Filter for single men in their twenties employed full time, and much of that state turns red.
insights.locator: And of course, even the Midwest

insights.claim: The author argues dating markets exist inside cultures, and that communities holding onto their values are best able to pass marriage-favoring norms to the next generation, so where marriage flourishes reflects local culture rather than pure supply-and-demand.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Framing family formation as culturally transmitted implies policy or market interventions on supply alone are insufficient to move marriage rates.
insights.locator: The obvious temptation is to make this a reflection on dating markets.

insights.claim: The author contends that when peers marry, put down roots, and start families, it becomes easier for others to envision that life, so local marriage rates are partly self-reinforcing through social norms.
insights.speaker: Danielle Franz
insights.so_what: Peer-driven normalization suggests marriage rates carry momentum and cluster, amplifying regional demographic divergence over time.
insights.quote: When your friends are getting married, putting down roots, and starting families, it becomes easier to envision that life for yourself.
